keyVerseText: And Elioenai, and Jaakobah, and Jeshohaiah, and Asaiah, and Adiel, and Jesimiel, and Benaiah,
rootMeaning: The name יְשִׁימָאֵל (Yᵉshîymâʼêl) derives from the Hebrew root שׂוּם (sûwm), which carries the idea of placing, appointing, or ordaining, combined with אֵל (El), meaning God. Thus, the literal sense of the name is "God will place" or "God will establish." This etymology conveys a divine action of God setting someone in a position or role, emphasizing God's sovereign authority in determining destiny and purpose beyond a mere personal identifier.
usageInScripture: The word יְשִׁימָאֵל appears only once in the canonical text, specifically in 1 Chronicles 4:36, where it is translated as Jesimiel or Jesimael. The sole occurrence identifies Jesimiel as a Simeonite chief, indicating a personal name linked to a tribal leader within Israel. The consistency of the translation as a proper name without variation highlights its function as a distinct individual rather than a concept or title.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding יְשִׁימָאֵל as "God will place" enriches our appreciation of how God sovereignly ordains individuals within His redemptive plan. Even a seemingly minor figure, such as a family chief named Jesimiel, bears a name that reflects God’s providential role in establishing His people’s leadership and heritage. This underscores the biblical truth that God is intimately involved in the lives and positions of His covenant people. Recognizing such names as theological affirmations invites believers to trust in God’s purposeful placement and governance over all aspects of life and history, ultimately fulfilled in Christ, who is the appointed King and Shepherd over God's people.
keyVerseReflection: In 1 Chronicles 4:36, Jesimiel is listed among other leaders, emphasizing his role within the Simeonite lineage. The inclusion of יְשִׁימָאֵל here highlights God’s provision and establishment of tribal leadership. The name itself, meaning "God will place," reminds readers that these leaders were not self-appointed but placed by divine authority, reinforcing the biblical theme of God’s sovereign orchestration of Israel’s history.
